script.opening: "Since I started those anti-inflammatory tablets for my knees a few weeks ago, I’ve had this burning indigestion and pain in the top of my stomach. Could you give me something for the acid? It’s really uncomfortable."

facts.text: Naproxen 500 mg twice a day, started 5 weeks ago by a locum for knee osteoarthritis. Helps the knees "a lot". Also takes low-dose aspirin 75 mg "that my old doctor started years ago for my heart, as a precaution" (only if all medicines are listed). Takes the naproxen sometimes on an empty stomach.
Started within a week of the naproxen. Burning in the top of the stomach, acid coming up, worse after meals and at night.
No vomiting, no blood or "coffee grounds", no black or tarry stools, no fainting. Swallowing fine. Weight steady. Not tired or breathless. No lumps.
Blood pressure — amlodipine. No previous ulcers. Never tested for H. pylori. Kidneys "fine last time". No allergies. Non-smoker; a glass of wine most evenings.
Osteoarthritis in both knees, worse over a year. Lives with husband. Looks after her grandchildren twice a week; walks the dog. "I don’t want to be back where I was, hobbling about."

Friendly, practical. Expect an acid tablet to take with the naproxen: "So can’t I just take an acid tablet with them?" Reluctant to lose the knee benefit; willing to try a gel and physiotherapy if explained. Surprised the aspirin matters.

ice.ideas: "The tablets are a bit strong for my stomach — an acid tablet will sort it."
ice.concerns: "I don’t want to stop the knee tablets — they’re the first thing that’s worked." Quietly worried about an ulcer, as her mother had one that bled.
ice.expectations: "Something for the acid so I can keep taking them."

cues: "Since I started those anti-inflammatory tablets" — the likely cause.
"Could you give me something for the acid?" — expectation of a PPI rather than a medication review.
"My old doctor started an aspirin" (if all medicines are asked) — a second gastrotoxic drug.

checkpoints.text: Recognises IATROGENIC (drug-induced) dyspepsia — linking onset to the medication (NSAID most commonly; aspirin/antiplatelets, bisphosphonates, steroids, SSRIs, iron, etc.)

Screens alarm features — GI bleeding (same-day hospital assessment, NICE CG141), anaemia, persistent vomiting, epigastric mass — and NICE NG12 upper-GI RED FLAGS (dysphagia, or age ≥55 with weight loss plus dyspepsia → suspected cancer pathway referral; age ≥55 with treatment-resistant dyspepsia → consider non-urgent direct-access endoscopy)

REVIEWS the medication and STOPS/SWITCHES the culprit where possible (e.g. stop the oral NSAID; topical NSAID and exercise for knee osteoarthritis per NICE NG226; lowest effective dose) — not reflexively adding a PPI on top
Provides GASTROPROTECTION (co-prescribe a PPI) only if a culprit (NSAID/antiplatelet) must continue, especially with risk factors, and considers H. pylori test-and-treat (after a 2-week PPI washout)
Gives lifestyle advice and REVIEWS response, escalating/endoscoping if persistent despite stopping the drug or if red flags emerge, and avoids long-term unreviewed PPIs
Explains why reviewing the drug (not just an acid tablet) is the right approach, and checks understanding
Negotiates the medication change with her (stopping or switching the culprit and finding alternative pain relief for her knees) rather than imposing it, and checks she is happy with the new plan

Safety-nets and follows up: red flags warranting a suspected cancer pathway referral or endoscopy under NICE NG12, alternative analgesia for her knees, gastroprotection if needed, H. pylori, and review — reviewing the medication, not masking with a PPI

worked.txt: "This indigestion started when you began the anti-inflammatory tablets, and that’s almost certainly the cause — they’re well known for irritating the stomach. So the best fix isn’t just an acid tablet on top; it’s to deal with the cause."

"First, a few important checks: any difficulty swallowing, weight loss, black or bloody stools, vomiting, or feeling a lump? … None. Good — at your age those would have needed an urgent specialist referral on the suspected cancer pathway, and any bleeding would mean hospital the same day."

"Let’s stop the anti-inflammatory tablets and manage your knees differently — an anti-inflammatory GEL rubbed on, which is much kinder to the stomach, and exercises to strengthen the thigh muscles, with physio if you’d like. That alone should settle the indigestion, and an acid-reducing tablet for four weeks will help it heal."

"If you ever genuinely need the tablet form, I’d add a stomach-protecting tablet alongside it, particularly given your age. If it comes back, I might also test for a stomach bug called H. pylori — that needs two weeks off the acid tablet first."
"Cutting back on things that trigger reflux — large/late meals, alcohol, smoking — helps too."

"If you vomit blood, pass black, tarry stools or feel faint, go to A&E or call 999 straight away. Come back sooner if you develop trouble swallowing, weight loss or keep vomiting, and otherwise I’ll see you in four weeks — those need prompt investigation."

f.learning: New DYSPEPSIA temporally linked to a medication change is often IATROGENIC (drug-induced), the commonest culprit being an NSAID, with others including aspirin/antiplatelets, oral bisphosphonates, corticosteroids, SSRIs, iron, calcium-channel blockers, nitrates and theophylline — so take a history linking onset to the drug. Critically, screen ALARM features that change management: GI bleeding (haematemesis/melaena, faintness or collapse) on an NSAID needs same-day hospital assessment as a possible bleeding ulcer (NICE CG141), not a referral pathway; iron-deficiency anaemia, persistent vomiting or an epigastric mass need clinical assessment; and, per NICE NG12 upper-GI, dysphagia at any age or age ≥55 with weight loss plus upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia — which warrants a suspected cancer pathway referral for oesophageal or stomach cancer (this replaced urgent direct-access endoscopy in 2025); age ≥55 with treatment-resistant dyspepsia warrants consideration of non-urgent direct-access endoscopy. The right action is to REVIEW the medication rather than reflexively add acid suppression: where possible stop/switch the culprit (e.g. stop the oral NSAID and use a topical NSAID with exercise and weight management for knee osteoarthritis — NICE NG226 advises against routinely offering paracetamol; lowest effective dose for the shortest time; reconsider the indication), because masking drug-induced symptoms with a PPI while continuing an ulcerogenic NSAID is poor practice. If an NSAID/antiplatelet must continue, co-prescribe a PPI for GASTROPROTECTION, especially with risk factors (age, previous ulcer/bleed, anticoagulants/steroids/SSRIs, H. pylori), and consider H. pylori test-and-treat (after 2 weeks off a PPI), with lifestyle advice (weight, alcohol, trigger foods, smoking). Manage per NICE CG184 (dyspepsia and GORD in adults), review the response, escalate/endoscope if dyspepsia persists despite stopping the drug or if red flags emerge, and avoid long-term unreviewed PPIs. The skill is recognising the drug cause, reviewing/rationalising medication rather than just adding a PPI, red-flag/NICE NG12 screening, and gastroprotection. NICE NG12 upper-GI applies where red-flag/age criteria are present.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE CG184 (2014, updated 2019) Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and dyspepsia in adults · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [3] NICE NG226 (2022) Osteoarthritis in over 16s · [4] NICE CG141 (2012) Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in over 16s · [5] BNF, NSAIDs and proton pump inhibitors
knowledge.summary: New dyspepsia that starts soon after a new NSAID is drug-induced until proved otherwise. Screen the upper-GI alarm features, stop or switch the culprit rather than adding a PPI on top, give short-term acid treatment and lifestyle advice, test for H. pylori if symptoms persist, and review. If an NSAID truly must continue, prescribe a PPI with it.

points.t: NICE CG184 asks you to review medicines that can cause dyspepsia, such as calcium antagonists, nitrates, theophyllines, bisphosphonates, corticosteroids and NSAIDs [1]. Aspirin, other antiplatelets, SSRIs and iron can also upset the stomach. A clear link in time between the new drug and the symptoms is the key history.

NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for oesophageal or stomach cancer if there is dysphagia, or age 55 and over with weight loss and upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia. Consider non-urgent direct-access endoscopy at 55 and over with treatment-resistant dyspepsia [2]. At 63, Mrs Devine meets the age part, so ask about weight loss and swallowing directly.

points.h: Bleeding is an emergency, not a referral
points.t: Haematemesis, melaena or collapse on an NSAID means possible bleeding peptic ulcer: arrange same-day hospital assessment [4]. Do not route bleeding through a routine or cancer pathway.

Stopping the oral NSAID treats the cause. For knee osteoarthritis, NICE NG226 puts therapeutic exercise and weight management first, offers a topical NSAID, and advises against routinely offering paracetamol or weak opioids [3]. Confirm the knee diagnosis at a later review.

For uninvestigated dyspepsia CG184 offers a full-dose PPI for 4 weeks or H. pylori test-and-treat [1]. Test for H. pylori only after 2 weeks without a PPI, and 4 weeks without antibiotics, or the result may be falsely negative [1]. Lifestyle advice: healthy weight, smoking, alcohol, and avoiding large or late meals.

Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time and prescribe a PPI with it [3][5]. Risk rises with age over 65, previous ulcer or bleed, and with anticoagulants, antiplatelets, corticosteroids or SSRIs. Oral NSAIDs also carry renal and cardiovascular risk [3][5].

points.h: Review, and don’t leave PPIs running
points.t: Review at about 4 weeks. If symptoms persist after the drug is stopped and treatment is given, or alarm features appear, investigate. Long-term PPIs should be reviewed at least yearly and stepped down to the lowest dose that controls symptoms, or stopped [1].

Impact of knee pain on mobility; why the NSAID was started and what she fears losing if it stops.

Drug-induced dyspepsia versus peptic ulcer, GORD, H. pylori, cardiac pain and upper-GI cancer.
Asks about dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting, haematemesis, melaena and anaemia symptoms; applies NICE NG12 at age 63.
NSAID-induced dyspepsia with no alarm features.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

Plans for knee pain (physiotherapy, NG226); gastroprotection if an NSAID must continue; records the adverse reaction.
999 or A&E for bleeding; earlier review for dysphagia, weight loss or vomiting; review at 4 weeks; H. pylori if symptoms return.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan

Idea (just acid), concern (the discomfort), expectation (a PPI to take alongside the NSAID).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.

When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, Mrs Devine, I’m Dr Shah. What can I do for you today?
model.why: Open question

model.text: Since I started those anti-inflammatory tablets for my knees a few weeks ago, I’ve had this burning indigestion and pain in the top of my stomach. Could you give me something for the acid? It’s really uncomfortable.
I’m sorry, that sounds miserable. I do want to help with the burning today. Can I ask a few questions first, so we get the right fix and not just a cover-up?
model.why: Acknowledges her request and sets the agenda

model.text: Of course.
Tell me about the indigestion. When did it start compared with the tablets, and where exactly is the pain?
model.why: Establishes the time link to the drug

model.text: Within a week or so of starting them. It’s here, at the top of my stomach, a burning, and some acid coming up.
Is the pain linked to effort, like walking uphill, or does it come with breathlessness or sweating?
model.why: Screens a cardiac mimic of epigastric pain

model.text: No, nothing like that. It’s worse after I eat.
Some important questions. Have you had any trouble swallowing, or food sticking? Have you lost weight without trying?
model.why: NICE NG12 upper-GI criteria at 63

model.text: No, swallowing’s fine, and my weight hasn’t changed.
Any vomiting, any blood when you’ve been sick, or black, tarry stools? And have you felt faint or more tired than usual?
model.why: Screens bleeding and anaemia

model.text: No, none of that.
Apart from the knee tablets, are you taking anything else, including aspirin, blood thinners, steroids, or anything you buy yourself?
model.why: Full medicine review, including over-the-counter drugs

model.text: It’s the knee tablets that are new. That’s the only thing that’s changed.
And how are your knees with the tablets? What does the pain stop you doing?
model.why: Explores the reason for the drug and its impact

model.text: They do help my knees, that’s the annoying thing. I don’t want to be back where I was, hobbling about.
So the tablets help your knees, but your stomach is paying for it. What were you hoping I’d do?
model.why: Explores expectation

model.text: I thought you’d just give me an acid tablet to go with them.
That’s a very reasonable thought. Is anything worrying you about the stomach pain itself?
model.why: Explores concerns

model.text: Not really. I just want it to stop.

From what you tell me, this is almost certainly caused by the anti-inflammatory tablets. They reduce the stomach’s own protective lining, which causes this burning, and in some people an ulcer or bleeding. At 63 the risk is higher.
model.why: Names drug-induced dyspepsia and explains why it matters

model.text: Oh. I didn’t know they could do that.

It’s very common. The reassuring part is that you have none of the warning signs I asked about: no swallowing trouble, weight loss, vomiting or bleeding. If you had, I’d be arranging an urgent specialist referral.
model.why: Explains the red-flag screen

model.text: That’s good. So can’t I just take an acid tablet with them?

We could, but that would hide the problem while the tablets carry on irritating your stomach. The better fix is to stop the anti-inflammatory tablets, which removes the cause. The burning usually settles once they’re stopped.
model.why: Treats the cause rather than masking it

model.text: I know your knees matter too, so let’s not leave you hobbling. An anti-inflammatory gel rubbed onto the knees works well for knee pain and very little reaches the stomach. Exercises to strengthen the thigh muscles help a lot as well. How would you feel about trying that?
model.why: Negotiates alternative knee treatment

model.text: I’d try the gel. I’m not sure about exercises, my knees ache.

That’s fair. I can refer you to a physiotherapist who will start gently. And for the burning, I’ll give you an acid-reducing tablet for four weeks while your stomach heals, then stop it. Does that sound fair?
model.why: Short PPI course for symptoms after the culprit is stopped

model.text: Yes, that’s what I wanted anyway. Only four weeks?

Yes. They’re useful short-term but shouldn’t run on without a review. If the indigestion comes back after that, I’ll test for a stomach bug called H. pylori. That needs two weeks off the acid tablet first, or it can give a false result.
model.why: H. pylori testing with the PPI washout

model.text: Right. And if I really need the knee tablets again?

Then we’d use the lowest dose for the shortest time, always with a stomach-protecting tablet alongside, and check your kidneys and blood pressure. Smaller, earlier evening meals and cutting down on alcohol also ease the burning.
model.why: Gastroprotection if an NSAID must continue; lifestyle

model.text: If you vomit blood, pass black, tarry stools or feel faint, go to A&E or call 999 straight away. Book to see me sooner if you have trouble swallowing, lose weight or keep vomiting. Otherwise I’ll see you in four weeks.
model.why: Bleeding emergency advice, NICE NG12 features, planned review

model.text: All right.
Could you tell me the plan in your own words, so I know I’ve explained it clearly?
model.why: Teach-back

model.text: Stop the anti-inflammatory tablets, use the gel and see the physio, take the acid tablet for four weeks, and come back if it doesn’t settle or I get those warning signs.
That’s exactly right. I’ll also add a note to your record about how these tablets affected you.
model.why: Confirms understanding; records the adverse reaction

social.t: Knee pain limits walking and daily tasks. Stopping her painkiller without a replacement plan leaves her worse off, so offer the alternative in the same consultation.
Ibuprofen and aspirin are sold widely. Tell her not to buy them as a substitute for the stopped tablets.

legal.t: Record the adverse reaction clearly in her notes. Suspected adverse drug reactions can be reported through the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices (2021): review medicines regularly and consider whether a new symptom is an adverse effect before adding another drug.
Time-limit PPI prescriptions and review long-term use at least annually (NICE CG184), rather than letting a short course become permanent.

community.t: Community pharmacists can reinforce the advice to avoid oral NSAIDs and explain gel use. Many areas allow self-referral to NHS physiotherapy for knee pain.

redFlags: Dysphagia, or age 55 and over with weight loss plus upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia: suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12)
Haematemesis, melaena, faintness: same-day hospital assessment (NICE CG141)
Persistent vomiting, symptoms of anaemia, epigastric mass
psychosocial: Reluctance to lose the pain relief that works
Expectation of a quick acid remedy
ice: Idea: she just needs something for the acid
Expectation: an acid tablet to take alongside the NSAID

playbook.diagnosis: “This is indigestion caused by the anti-inflammatory tablets, with none of the warning signs of anything more serious.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your stomach has a protective coating, a bit like the non-stick layer on a pan. Anti-inflammatory tablets scrape away at that coating, so the acid starts to burn. An acid tablet turns the heat down, but stopping the tablets stops the scraping.”

management.reflectIce: “You came for an acid tablet, and I will give you one for a few weeks. But the real fix is to stop the tablets causing it and treat your knees in a way that’s kinder to your stomach.”
management.psychosocial: Keep her mobile: offer the knee alternative before asking her to give up the NSAID, and check she accepts it.
sharedPlan: Stop the oral NSAID and record the adverse reaction
Topical NSAID and therapeutic exercise or physiotherapy for the knees (NICE NG226)
Full-dose PPI for 4 weeks, then stop (NICE CG184; dose per BNF)
H. pylori test if symptoms return, after 2 weeks off the PPI
If an NSAID must restart: lowest dose, shortest time, with a PPI; check renal function and blood pressure
safetyNet: 999 or A&E for vomiting blood, black stools or faintness
Return sooner for dysphagia, weight loss or persistent vomiting (NICE NG12)

pitfalls.intro: This station is lost by treating the symptom and not the cause, by an incomplete alarm screen, and by taking away her knee relief without a replacement. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Adding a PPI and leaving the NSAID running.
items.why: NICE CG184 asks you to review medicines that cause dyspepsia; masking symptoms keeps ulcer and bleeding risk.
items.fix: Stop or switch the NSAID; use a PPI short-term, or with the NSAID only if it truly must continue.

items.fail: Skipping weight loss and dysphagia questions because the drug explains everything.
items.why: At 63, weight loss with dyspepsia or any dysphagia needs a suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12).
items.fix: Ask both questions directly and document the answers.

items.fail: Quoting urgent direct-access endoscopy for alarm features.
items.why: The 2025 NICE NG12 amendment changed these to suspected cancer pathway referrals.
items.fix: Use current wording: suspected cancer pathway referral; non-urgent endoscopy for treatment-resistant dyspepsia at 55 and over.

items.fail: Testing for H. pylori while she is taking a PPI.
items.why: PPIs can cause false-negative results; CG184 requires a 2-week washout.
items.fix: Test before starting the PPI, or 2 weeks after stopping it.

items.fail: Telling her to stop the tablets with no plan for her knees.
items.why: She values the pain relief; she may buy ibuprofen instead.
items.fix: Offer a topical NSAID and exercise or physiotherapy, and agree the plan with her.

items.fail: Vague safety-net: “come back if it gets worse”.
items.why: GI bleeding on an NSAID is an emergency.
items.fix: Name haematemesis, melaena and faintness as 999 or A&E triggers; book a 4-week review; teach-back.

timeMap.d: Hear the story and the request for an acid tablet; agree to look for the cause first.
Time link to the NSAID, pain character, cardiac screen, dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting, bleeding, full medicine list, knee impact.
Expects a PPI alongside the NSAID; wants the burning to stop.
Drug-induced dyspepsia; no alarm features; why stopping beats masking.
Stop NSAID, topical NSAID and physio, 4-week PPI, H. pylori if it recurs, gastroprotection if an NSAID restarts, bleeding safety-net, review, teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes a PPI to take with the NSAID and ends the consultation; no questions about swallowing, weight or bleeding; no plan for her knees.
wordPics.pass: Links the dyspepsia to the NSAID, screens alarm features, stops the NSAID with an alternative for the knees, and safety-nets for bleeding.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: applies NICE NG12 age criteria precisely; offers a time-limited PPI and explains the H. pylori washout; negotiates knee care using NG226 rather than defaulting to paracetamol; plans gastroprotection if an NSAID must restart; records the adverse reaction; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Here’s an acid tablet to take with your anti-inflammatories.”
avoid.instead: “The tablets are causing this, so the best fix is to stop them and treat your knees another way.”
avoid.why: A PPI alone hides the cause while ulcer and bleeding risk continue.

avoid.dont: “If it gets worse we’ll send you for an urgent camera test.”
avoid.instead: “If you have trouble swallowing or lose weight, come back and I’ll refer you urgently to the specialists.”
avoid.why: NICE NG12 now uses a suspected cancer pathway referral, not urgent direct-access endoscopy, for these features.

avoid.dont: “Just take regular paracetamol for your knees instead.”
avoid.instead: “A gel on the knees and strengthening exercises are the best next steps.”
avoid.why: NICE NG226 advises against routinely offering paracetamol for osteoarthritis.

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d try the gel. I’m not sure about exercises, my knees ache.

That’s fair. I can refer you to a physiotherapist who will start gently. And for the burning, I’ll give you an acid-reducing tablet for four weeks while your stomach heals, then stop it. Does that sound fair?
SCA_MODELS.why: Short PPI course for symptoms after the culprit is stopped

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, that’s what I wanted anyway. Only four weeks?

Yes. They’re useful short-term but shouldn’t run on without a review. If the indigestion comes back after that, I’ll test for a stomach bug called H. pylori. That needs two weeks off the acid tablet first, or it can give a false result.
SCA_MODELS.why: H. pylori testing with the PPI washout

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. And if I really need the knee tablets again?

Then we’d use the lowest dose for the shortest time, always with a stomach-protecting tablet alongside, and check your kidneys and blood pressure. Smaller, earlier evening meals and cutting down on alcohol also ease the burning.
SCA_MODELS.why: Gastroprotection if an NSAID must continue; lifestyle

SCA_MODELS.text: If you vomit blood, pass black, tarry stools or feel faint, go to A&E or call 999 straight away. Book to see me sooner if you have trouble swallowing, lose weight or keep vomiting. Otherwise I’ll see you in four weeks.
SCA_MODELS.why: Bleeding emergency advice, NICE NG12 features, planned review

SCA_MODELS.text: All right.
Could you tell me the plan in your own words, so I know I’ve explained it clearly?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Stop the anti-inflammatory tablets, use the gel and see the physio, take the acid tablet for four weeks, and come back if it doesn’t settle or I get those warning signs.
That’s exactly right. I’ll also add a note to your record about how these tablets affected you.
SCA_MODELS.why: Confirms understanding; records the adverse reaction

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE CG184 (2014, updated 2019) Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and dyspepsia in adults · NICE NG12 Suspected cancer: recognition and referral (2015, last updated 15 April 2026) · [3] NICE NG226 (2022) Osteoarthritis in over 16s · [4] NICE CG141 (2012) Acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding in over 16s · [5] BNF, NSAIDs and proton pump inhibitors
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: New dyspepsia that starts soon after a new NSAID is drug-induced until proved otherwise. Screen the upper-GI alarm features, stop or switch the culprit rather than adding a PPI on top, give short-term acid treatment and lifestyle advice, test for H. pylori if symptoms persist, and review. If an NSAID truly must continue, prescribe a PPI with it.

points.t: NICE CG184 asks you to review medicines that can cause dyspepsia, such as calcium antagonists, nitrates, theophyllines, bisphosphonates, corticosteroids and NSAIDs [1]. Aspirin, other antiplatelets, SSRIs and iron can also upset the stomach. A clear link in time between the new drug and the symptoms is the key history.

NICE NG12: refer on a suspected cancer pathway for oesophageal or stomach cancer if there is dysphagia, or age 55 and over with weight loss and upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia. Consider non-urgent direct-access endoscopy at 55 and over with treatment-resistant dyspepsia [2]. At 63, Mrs Devine meets the age part, so ask about weight loss and swallowing directly.

points.h: Bleeding is an emergency, not a referral
points.t: Haematemesis, melaena or collapse on an NSAID means possible bleeding peptic ulcer: arrange same-day hospital assessment [4]. Do not route bleeding through a routine or cancer pathway.

Stopping the oral NSAID treats the cause. For knee osteoarthritis, NICE NG226 puts therapeutic exercise and weight management first, offers a topical NSAID, and advises against routinely offering paracetamol or weak opioids [3]. Confirm the knee diagnosis at a later review.

For uninvestigated dyspepsia CG184 offers a full-dose PPI for 4 weeks or H. pylori test-and-treat [1]. Test for H. pylori only after 2 weeks without a PPI, and 4 weeks without antibiotics, or the result may be falsely negative [1]. Lifestyle advice: healthy weight, smoking, alcohol, and avoiding large or late meals.

Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time and prescribe a PPI with it [3][5]. Risk rises with age over 65, previous ulcer or bleed, and with anticoagulants, antiplatelets, corticosteroids or SSRIs. Oral NSAIDs also carry renal and cardiovascular risk [3][5].

points.h: Review, and don’t leave PPIs running
points.t: Review at about 4 weeks. If symptoms persist after the drug is stopped and treatment is given, or alarm features appear, investigate. Long-term PPIs should be reviewed at least yearly and stepped down to the lowest dose that controls symptoms, or stopped [1].

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; lets her link the burning pain to the new knee tablets in her own words.
Impact of knee pain on mobility; why the NSAID was started and what she fears losing if it stops.
Picks up “since I started those tablets” as the key cue; hears that the NSAID helps her knees.
Idea (just acid), concern (the discomfort), expectation (a PPI to take alongside the NSAID).
Checks alarm features at the bedside; considers knee review and renal function and blood pressure if an NSAID is restarted; H. pylori test only after a PPI washout.
Drug-induced dyspepsia versus peptic ulcer, GORD, H. pylori, cardiac pain and upper-GI cancer.
Asks about dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting, haematemesis, melaena and anaemia symptoms; applies NICE NG12 at age 63.
NSAID-induced dyspepsia with no alarm features.
Stops the oral NSAID; topical NSAID and exercise for the knees; 4-week PPI then stop; lifestyle advice.
Plans for knee pain (physiotherapy, NG226); gastroprotection if an NSAID must continue; records the adverse reaction.
999 or A&E for bleeding; earlier review for dysphagia, weight loss or vomiting; review at 4 weeks; H. pylori if symptoms return.

social.t: Knee pain limits walking and daily tasks. Stopping her painkiller without a replacement plan leaves her worse off, so offer the alternative in the same consultation.
Ibuprofen and aspirin are sold widely. Tell her not to buy them as a substitute for the stopped tablets.

legal.t: Record the adverse reaction clearly in her notes. Suspected adverse drug reactions can be reported through the MHRA Yellow Card scheme.

professional.t: GMC Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices (2021): review medicines regularly and consider whether a new symptom is an adverse effect before adding another drug.
Time-limit PPI prescriptions and review long-term use at least annually (NICE CG184), rather than letting a short course become permanent.

community.t: Community pharmacists can reinforce the advice to avoid oral NSAIDs and explain gel use. Many areas allow self-referral to NHS physiotherapy for knee pain.

redFlags: Dysphagia, or age 55 and over with weight loss plus upper abdominal pain, reflux or dyspepsia: suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12)
Haematemesis, melaena, faintness: same-day hospital assessment (NICE CG141)
Persistent vomiting, symptoms of anaemia, epigastric mass
psychosocial: Reluctance to lose the pain relief that works
Expectation of a quick acid remedy
ice: Idea: she just needs something for the acid
Expectation: an acid tablet to take alongside the NSAID

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is indigestion caused by the anti-inflammatory tablets, with none of the warning signs of anything more serious.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your stomach has a protective coating, a bit like the non-stick layer on a pan. Anti-inflammatory tablets scrape away at that coating, so the acid starts to burn. An acid tablet turns the heat down, but stopping the tablets stops the scraping.”

management.reflectIce: “You came for an acid tablet, and I will give you one for a few weeks. But the real fix is to stop the tablets causing it and treat your knees in a way that’s kinder to your stomach.”
management.psychosocial: Keep her mobile: offer the knee alternative before asking her to give up the NSAID, and check she accepts it.
sharedPlan: Stop the oral NSAID and record the adverse reaction
Topical NSAID and therapeutic exercise or physiotherapy for the knees (NICE NG226)
Full-dose PPI for 4 weeks, then stop (NICE CG184; dose per BNF)
H. pylori test if symptoms return, after 2 weeks off the PPI
If an NSAID must restart: lowest dose, shortest time, with a PPI; check renal function and blood pressure
safetyNet: 999 or A&E for vomiting blood, black stools or faintness
Return sooner for dysphagia, weight loss or persistent vomiting (NICE NG12)

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is lost by treating the symptom and not the cause, by an incomplete alarm screen, and by taking away her knee relief without a replacement. Each pattern below is common and fixable.

items.fail: Adding a PPI and leaving the NSAID running.
items.why: NICE CG184 asks you to review medicines that cause dyspepsia; masking symptoms keeps ulcer and bleeding risk.
items.fix: Stop or switch the NSAID; use a PPI short-term, or with the NSAID only if it truly must continue.

items.fail: Skipping weight loss and dysphagia questions because the drug explains everything.
items.why: At 63, weight loss with dyspepsia or any dysphagia needs a suspected cancer pathway referral (NICE NG12).
items.fix: Ask both questions directly and document the answers.

items.fail: Quoting urgent direct-access endoscopy for alarm features.
items.why: The 2025 NICE NG12 amendment changed these to suspected cancer pathway referrals.
items.fix: Use current wording: suspected cancer pathway referral; non-urgent endoscopy for treatment-resistant dyspepsia at 55 and over.

items.fail: Testing for H. pylori while she is taking a PPI.
items.why: PPIs can cause false-negative results; CG184 requires a 2-week washout.
items.fix: Test before starting the PPI, or 2 weeks after stopping it.

items.fail: Telling her to stop the tablets with no plan for her knees.
items.why: She values the pain relief; she may buy ibuprofen instead.
items.fix: Offer a topical NSAID and exercise or physiotherapy, and agree the plan with her.

items.fail: Vague safety-net: “come back if it gets worse”.
items.why: GI bleeding on an NSAID is an emergency.
items.fix: Name haematemesis, melaena and faintness as 999 or A&E triggers; book a 4-week review; teach-back.
